subject: Accounting
title: Benford's Law: Math Catches Fraud
description: A quick, practical guide to Benford's Law: Math Catches Fraud.

hook.text: In real financial data, the digit 1 appears first about 30% of the time. Faked data doesn't follow this.

buildup.text: Benford's Law predicts the frequency of leading digits in naturally occurring datasets.

discovery.text: Forensic accountants use Benford's Law to scan thousands of transactions for anomalies.

twist.text: Fraudsters who fabricate numbers usually distribute digits too evenly—math betrays them.

climax.text: It's been used in court cases and tax audits worldwide to flag suspicious records.

punchline.text: Math has a pattern. Liars break it.

quiz.question: What does Benford's Law predict?
options: The frequency of leading digits in real data

details.summary: Benford's Law states that in naturally occurring datasets, the digit 1 appears as the leading digit about 30% of the time—not the expected 11%. This topic explains how forensic accountants use this mathematical property to detect fabricated financial data.
details.whyItMatters: Fraudsters who invent numbers typically distribute digits evenly, which creates a statistical fingerprint that doesn't match natural data. Benford's Law makes fabricated data mathematically detectable.
takeaways: Naturally occurring numbers start with 1 about 30% of the time, with 9 less than 5% of the time
Financial data that deviates significantly from Benford's distribution may indicate manipulation
The law works best on large datasets of naturally growing numbers like revenues and expenses

faq.question: What is Benford's Law and how does it detect fraud?
faq.answer: Benford's Law predicts that in natural datasets, lower leading digits appear more frequently than higher ones—1 appears about 30% of the time, 9 only about 5%. When financial data deviates from this pattern, it may indicate numbers were fabricated or manipulated.

faq.question: Does Benford's Law work on all financial data?
faq.answer: It works best on large datasets of numbers that span several orders of magnitude, like invoices, revenues, or population figures. It doesn't apply to assigned numbers (zip codes, phone numbers) or data constrained to a narrow range (hourly wages, room rates).
